Reputation Crisis Playbook: What to Do in the First 48 Hours

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

The first 48 hours of a reputation crisis decide whether it stays a contained incident or becomes the story people remember about your company. In that window the goal is not to win the argument but to take control: appoint who decides, publish a short holding statement, monitor what is spreading, avoid the classic mistakes and document everything for later legal or platform action.

What the first 48 hours of reputation crisis management are for

Effective reputation crisis management in the first two days is about stabilising the situation, not resolving it. You rarely know all the facts at hour one, and any attempt to give a complete answer too early tends to produce corrections later, which feed a second wave of coverage.

A simple timeline helps the team understand what is expected and when. It works equally for a viral post about a restaurant in Rome, a product defect reported by an Italian consumer association or an employee video circulating on TikTok.

WindowPriorityOutput
Hours 0–2Confirm the facts that are known, convene the crisis cellNamed decision owner, first internal brief
Hours 2–6Publish a holding statement, pause scheduled contentStatement on owned channels, briefing for front-line staff
Hours 6–24Monitor spread, answer key stakeholders directlyMonitoring log, Q&A document, first update
Hours 24–48Substantive update, decide on legal and platform actionsSecond statement, evidence file, plan for the following weeks

Who decides: setting up the crisis cell

One person must have the final word on every public statement. Crises in Italian companies often stall because the founder, the commercial director and the external press office each publish their own version, and the contradictions become the news.

The crisis cell should be small enough to meet in fifteen minutes and include only people who can act. A typical composition is:

  • a decision owner, usually the CEO or managing director, who approves every external message;
  • a communications lead who drafts statements and handles journalists;
  • legal counsel, internal or external, who checks statements and evaluates defamation, privacy or consumer-law issues;
  • an operations or customer-service lead who knows the facts on the ground and can fix the underlying problem;
  • a monitoring owner who tracks mentions, reviews and search results and reports at fixed intervals;
  • a single spokesperson, who may coincide with the decision owner but must be one face only.

Give everyone else in the company a short internal note: what happened, that a statement is coming, and that nobody comments externally or on personal social accounts. In Italy, where many staff are active on Facebook and local WhatsApp groups, this single message prevents a large share of accidental leaks.

The holding statement: say little, say it fast

A holding statement is a short, factual message published within a few hours that shows you are aware, taking the matter seriously and will provide more information. It buys time without committing you to details you have not verified.

Good holding statements share the same structure: acknowledgement of the issue in plain words, an expression of concern for anyone affected, what you are doing right now, and when the next update will come. They avoid speculation, blame on customers or employees, and legal language. Publish it where the conversation is happening, typically your website, the social channel where the issue started and, if relevant, a reply on the review platform, in Italian and, for international brands, in English as well.

Front-line staff need the same message. Shop assistants, call-centre operators and sales agents will be asked about the incident; a two-line script aligned with the statement keeps your online crisis management consistent with what customers hear on the phone or at the counter.

Monitoring: know what is spreading and where

Monitoring in a crisis has one purpose: to tell the decision owner whether the situation is growing, stable or fading, and which audience is driving it. Without this information every decision is a guess.

Track mentions of the brand and of the people involved across social networks, news sites, forums and review platforms, plus Google results and autocomplete for the company name. Record new reviews on Google Business Profile, Trustpilot or TripAdvisor separately, because review bombing often follows a viral post. Report at fixed times, for example every three hours on day one, with a short note on volume, tone, key sources and any journalist enquiries. Mistakes that make a crisis worse

Most crises are amplified by the company's own reaction rather than by the original incident. The errors below appear again and again, and each is avoidable.

  • Deleting critical comments in bulk or disabling them, which is screenshotted and becomes evidence of a cover-up.
  • Public legal threats against customers or journalists before counsel has assessed the content.
  • Arguing in comment threads, where every reply adds visibility to the original post.
  • Continuing scheduled promotional posts and newsletters as if nothing were happening.
  • Giving different versions to different journalists, or speaking off the record without preparation.
  • Buying positive reviews or followers to dilute criticism, which breaks platform rules and is easily detected.

Individual replies still matter, but they should be calm, short and consistent with the statement. The principles in our guide on responding to negative reviews apply equally to comments during a crisis.

Escalation and documentation

From the first hour, everything must be documented as if it will be needed in court, because sometimes it will. Screenshots with visible URL, date and time, saved copies of posts and articles, and a log of every decision and statement form the basis of any later reputation crisis response through platforms or the law.

For content that may be defamatory under art. 595 c.p., a certified copy of web pages made by a notary or a forensic specialist carries far more weight than a simple screenshot, and it should be obtained before the author deletes or edits the post. Keep in mind that a criminal complaint (querela) must generally be filed within three months of learning of the offence. If the crisis involves a personal data breach, the GDPR requires notification to the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to create a risk for individuals.

Escalate beyond the crisis cell when the issue touches safety, regulators, the Polizia Postale or listed-company disclosure duties. For content clearly illegal under the Digital Services Act, platforms must provide a notice mechanism; use it with precise references to each URL rather than general complaints.

In the first 48 hours, speed matters for the holding statement and for evidence. Everything else benefits from one more hour of verification.

From hour 48 to recovery

By the end of day two you should know whether the crisis is fading or entering a longer phase. If it is fading, publish a substantive update explaining what happened and what has changed, then gradually return to normal communication. If it is growing, the focus moves to a structured plan: stakeholder outreach, removal or delisting of unlawful content, and new, accurate content that restores a balanced page one. Our case study on recovery after a viral negative post shows how that next phase looks in practice.

Preparation is what makes the first 48 hours manageable. Companies that have a named crisis cell, statement templates and a monitoring set-up before anything happens react in hours rather than days.
